text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(a) What does the conjunctive vav in the word “And in the year” indicate? By what means did Hashem stir his spirit? And why both a proclamation and a written decree?
text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: “And in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia”—Ezra [who wrote his own book and the Book of Chronicles] concluded at the end of Chronicles: “And he exiled the remnant to Babylon, and they became servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfill the word of Hashem spoken by Jeremiah, until the land had appeased its Sabbaths; throughout all the days of its desolation it rested, to fulfill seventy years. And in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, in order to complete the word of Hashem spoken by Jeremiah, Hashem stirred the spirit of Cyrus,” etc., through, “Whoever among you is of all His people—Hashem his God be with him, and let him go up.” It is evident that the Book of Ezra was written after the Book of Chronicles; therefore, Ezra began this book with the final two verses with which he concluded his previous book. He consequently said “And in the year,” with a conjunctive vav, because this is a continuation of the Book of Chronicles [this is also the opinion of Don Isaac Abarbanel]. The meaning is that Jeremiah’s prophecy explicitly stated that the decree of restoration would occur at the time of Babylon’s destruction, which was seventy years after the beginning of the Babylonian kingdom, as explained there [Jeremiah 25:12; 29:10]. However, because they were punished with seventy years of exile for having neglected the sabbatical years, the reckoning should have begun with the exile of Zedekiah, which occurred eighteen years after the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, for it was from then that the land lay desolate and appeased its Sabbaths. The angel revealed this to Daniel in the third vision [Daniel 9:24], when he said, “Seventy weeks have been decreed upon your people,” as I explained there. Daniel therefore understood from the books that the reckoning had to be “for the completion of the desolations of Jerusalem,” as stated there [Daniel 9:2]. Both reckonings were fulfilled. To fulfill the word of Hashem spoken by Jeremiah, Hashem stirred the spirit of Cyrus in the first year of his reign, and Cyrus issued a decree permitting the people to return to Jerusalem and build the Temple. This decree was intended only to fulfill Jeremiah’s statement that, upon the completion of Babylon’s seventy years, “I will fulfill My good word concerning you, to return you to this place.” Jeremiah did not promise there that the Temple would then be built, for the proper time for that had not yet arrived. That time would come only eighteen years later, upon the completion of the seventy years from Jerusalem’s destruction, when atonement for the sin of neglecting the sabbatical years would be complete. However, had Cyrus not granted permission to build the Temple, the people would not have returned from exile. Therefore, Hashem stirred his spirit to grant permission to build the Temple; as a result, many returned from Babylon, and Jeremiah’s words were fulfilled. The building was subsequently halted until the second year of Darius, who again granted permission, thereby fulfilling the words, “until the land had appeased its Sabbaths,” whose reckoning began at the time of the destruction. This is what the end of Chronicles means: to fulfill the word of Hashem spoken by Jeremiah—which required them to return immediately at the beginning of Cyrus’s reign—and to fulfill “until the land had appeased its Sabbaths,” which was not completed until eighteen years later. Therefore, in the first year of Cyrus, Hashem stirred his spirit. The Book of Ezra thus continues and completes the Book of Chronicles: it relates that the exiles then went up and Jeremiah’s words were fulfilled; afterward, it relates how construction was halted and how they resumed building eighteen years later, in the second year of Darius, thereby fulfilling “until the land had appeased its Sabbaths.” “Hashem stirred the spirit of Cyrus”—it is explained in Josippon that when Daniel interpreted for Belshazzar the writing declaring that the king would be punished because Belshazzar had desecrated the vessels of the Temple, and Belshazzar was killed that very night and Darius the Mede received his kingdom, these events became known to Darius and Cyrus, and they vowed to rebuild the Temple. It may also be said that Cyrus learned of Isaiah’s prophecy concerning him: “He shall build My city and release My exiles.” These words of Hashem stirred his spirit. “And he caused a proclamation to pass throughout his entire kingdom, and also in writing”—he had it publicly proclaimed aloud, and he also issued the decree in writing, because a decree not committed to writing could be altered. But a document written in the king’s name could not be revoked under the laws of Media and Persia [as explained in Esther and in Daniel, chapter 6]. The later suspension of the building did not constitute a change to this decree, as will be explained in chapter 4. Moreover, because of this written document, they were able to begin building again in the days of the latter Darius, as stated below [Ezra 6:1–2].
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: “All the kingdoms”—He made known that he believed there is a God in heaven who rules over everything. He called Him only “the God of heaven” because he thought that God entrusted the governance of the earth to the one appointed to act in His place, and that he himself had been chosen by Hashem to govern on His behalf upon the earth, who had delivered the kingdoms of the earth into his hand. He had also “charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem,” because there He desired to establish His dwelling among the people who worship Him.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(3–4) Why did he say, “He is the God who is in Jerusalem”? What did he mean by saying, “And whoever remains,” and by saying, “Let the people of his place assist him”?
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: “Whoever among you”—He said this to the nations: Whoever is found among you from among all His people—for since the building of His Temple is possible only through His people, you must send them there. “May Hashem his God be with him,” meaning that Divine assistance and heavenly inspiration should accompany him: both for the ascent to Jerusalem, concerning which he said, “Let him go up to Jerusalem,” and for the building, concerning which he said, “And let him build the house of Hashem, the God of Israel.” His meaning was that concerning the future it is written, “For My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples,” and He will not be called specifically the God of Israel, because all peoples will worship Him. But the time for this had not yet arrived. Therefore, he said, “He is the God who is in Jerusalem” alone, because, in his view, God had entrusted the governance of the entire world outside Jerusalem to the celestial order. He then said that whoever was moved of his own accord to go up and build should go; however—
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “And whoever remains”—Whoever is not moved to go and remains outside the Land—whether because his spirit is lowly and does not rise to this great undertaking, because he lacks the expenses, or because he has nothing to contribute toward the building of the Temple—concerning him Cyrus commanded that whoever remains, in whatever place he resides, should be assisted by the people of his place: (1) They should support him with silver and gold, with goods having monetary value, and with animals upon which to ride; (2) they should uplift him, which also means that they should inspire his spirit to undertake this journey; and (3) together with the voluntary offering—the nations should send through him a consecrated donation for the House of God.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then they arose”—Scripture relates that there were two aspects to this. First, the people elevated themselves toward this undertaking of their own accord, led by the heads of the ancestral houses of Judah and Benjamin, who were the first to be awakened to it. Thus there was an awakening from below—“then they arose”—and from this came an awakening from above, for everyone—that is, everyone who went up—was one whose spirit God had stirred, both to go up and to build the House of Hashem. Nevertheless, all those around them—that is, the neighboring peoples—also strengthened their hands. [“Strengthening weak hands” is always expressed with the hands as the direct object. Here, however, they did not require strengthening because their hands were weak; rather, the people strengthened them through gifts, enabling them to be even stronger. Therefore, the phrase is constructed with the preposition “in.”] Besides means that everything mentioned thus far was given for the needs of those going up—their provisions and traveling expenses—apart from the donations that were sent through them for the Temple.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: The question (7–8): Why is the verb “brought out” repeated—“Cyrus brought out” and “Mithredath brought them out”?
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: “And King Cyrus brought out,” etc., “and he brought them out”—Because the vessels had been kept in a temple of idols, and it would otherwise have been impossible to use them again in the Temple, Scripture relates that Cyrus first brought them out of the idolatrous temple and delivered them to the treasurer. This constituted a kind of nullification of their idolatrous status, since they passed from the possession of the idol to the possession of the king. The king then had his treasurer bring them out from his own possession and count them out to Sheshbazzar.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “Agartalei”—According to our Sages, these were a kind of basin. “Mahalafim”—knives. “Kephorim”—a kind of basin; see Rashi. “Of a second rank”—they were one grade below the preceding ones, as in, “the best of the sheep and those of the second rank” (I Samuel 15).
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “All the vessels”—In addition to the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken out, Cyrus also donated vessels, and altogether there were five thousand four hundred.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “Now these are the people of the province”—This passage is repeated in Nehemiah [chapter 7], with many variations. In some cases, the number given there is smaller than the number here: for example, the descendants of Arah number seven hundred here and six hundred there; the descendants of Zattu number nine hundred here and eight hundred there. In most cases, however, the number there is greater: the descendants of Azgad number one thousand here and two thousand there; the descendants of Adin number four hundred here and six hundred there, and so forth. It appears that the present passage speaks of the prominent people who went up from Babylon itself. When Jehoiachin was exiled, Nebuchadnezzar exiled the officials and the leading members of the nation. He brought them to the capital, where they were always treated with honor. Those exiled with Zedekiah, however, were sent throughout the provinces, because they were lowly in his eyes, as described [in Jeremiah 24] by the good figs and the bad figs. Here it says, “whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled to Babylon,” whereas there it merely says, “whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled.” This is because the present passage speaks of those exiled with Jehoiachin, who were brought to Babylon itself, the capital city, while the passage there speaks of those exiled with Zedekiah, who were sent to the provincial cities. The prominent people discussed here had Jerusalem as their principal destination, and from there they spread throughout Judah. The less prominent people had Judah as their principal destination, intending to settle there. Therefore, here it says “to Jerusalem and Judah,” without repeating the preposition “to” before Judah, whereas there it says “to Jerusalem and to Judah,” using the preposition for both. This accords with what I wrote in my commentary HaTorah VeHaMitzvah [on the portion of Aharei Mot, concerning the verse “and a ram for a burnt offering”]: wherever the preposition is not repeated, the first element is primary; when it is repeated, both elements are equal. Here it says that they “came with Zerubbabel,” etc., whereas there it adds Azariah, Raamiah, and Nahamani, who arrived later with additional groups of people. Therefore, the number counted there is greater than the number here. In the few cases where the number counted here is greater, the difference consists of those who returned from the Land of Israel to Babylon after construction was halted; their number was consequently absent from the second count, which was made later. [See further below, verse 64.]
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: “Who came”—to Jerusalem. “Mordecai Bilshan”—according to our Sages, this refers to one person: Mordecai, who knew many languages. According to some commentators, however, these are two separate names. “Mispar”—the first form is a personal name; in Nehemiah, it appears as “Mispereth.”
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(6–35) This passage is repeated in Nehemiah (chapter 7), where there are many variations and different numbers. In some cases, the number there is greater, while in others it is smaller than the number given here.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: “The descendants of Pahath-moab, of the descendants of Jeshua”—Pahath-moab was the head of the family, and the descendants of two of his sons, Jeshua and Joab, came to the Land of Israel. The same construction appears in verses 16, 36, and 40. This is necessarily so from what is stated in verse 40: “The descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the house of Hodaviah,” which is identical to what is stated [in Ezra 3:9]: “Jeshua and his sons and brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the descendants of Judah.”
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: “The people of Bethlehem”—Those who all belonged to one family, even if they lived in several cities, were counted together under the name of the head of their family. If they did not belong to a single family, they were grouped according to the city in which they had formerly lived.
text.1_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: “The people of Anathoth”—See what I have written on Jeremiah [16:3].
text.1_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: “The descendants of the other Elam”—The descendants of Elam were already counted [in verse 7]; however, this was a different man, and it happened that the number of people in his family was equal to that of the first Elam’s family.
text.1_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: “The priests”—After enumerating the Israelites, he enumerated the priests and Levites. Among the Levites, he counted the singers and the gatekeepers; afterward, he counted the Temple servants, who served the priests.
text.1_Chapter, 54_Verse, 0_Comment: “The descendants of Solomon’s servants”—According to one opinion in Yevamot, which holds that the child of a non-Jew or a slave and a Jewish woman is a mamzer, they were mamzerim, because Solomon’s servants married Jewish women and had children by them. They therefore belong with those listed afterward whose parentage was uncertain—the shetuki and the asufi—as stated in Kiddushin: “Ten genealogical classes went up from Babylon.” According to the opinion that the child is legitimate, it may be said that they were included among the emancipated slaves. As Tosafot explain in Yevamot [16b], because their owners had despaired of recovering them, they did not require documents of emancipation. They were thus included among the converts and freedmen counted among the ten genealogical classes. Since they are counted together with the Temple servants, it appears that they descended from the seven Canaanite nations whom Solomon subjected to forced labor, as stated in II Chronicles [8:7]. “The descendants of Hassophereth”—The initial heh is not the definite article but an integral part of the name, as I have demonstrated similarly in I Chronicles 2:52 and elsewhere.
text.1_Chapter, 58_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they could not state their ancestral house or their descent”—That is, they could not identify their ancestral house—namely, the family from which they came—and they could not even establish their descent, whether they were Israelites at all, because they had been taken in from the street in a place where the majority of the population was non-Jewish. This also implies that they did not know whether they were of legitimate birth or were mamzerim, corresponding to the shetuki and the asufi included among the ten genealogical classes.
text.1_Chapter, 60_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(61) Why does Scripture relate that he took a wife from the daughters of Barzillai and was called by their name?
text.1_Chapter, 60_Verse, 1_Comment: “The descendants of Hakkoz, the descendants of Barzillai”—That is, the family of Hakkoz consisted of priests, and they are mentioned in Chronicles [I Chronicles 24:19] as the seventh house in the order of the priestly divisions. Now, however, doubt arose concerning some of his descendants. The reason was that Hakkoz had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai, who were prominent in the days of David and Solomon, and the sons born from this woman were also honorably called by the name of Barzillai. It may be that Habaiah was the son born from this woman, and his descendants had two names: they were called both the descendants of Hakkoz and the descendants of Barzillai. Scripture explains that this was because he took—that is, Hakkoz took—a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and he was called—that is, Habaiah, who was born from this woman, was called—by their name. He was named both after his father and after his maternal grandfather, and his descendants were therefore called both the descendants of Hakkoz and the descendants of Barzillai. As long as their genealogical register remained in their possession, this created no difficulty. But they sought their genealogical record, but it could not be found. Their genealogical documents were no longer available. [Each family possessed a general genealogical register covering the entire family, while individuals also possessed separate documents recording their own particular lineage. Neither their collective family record—which is why “their record” is expressed in the singular—nor their individual genealogical records—which is why “they were not found” is expressed in the plural—could be found.] Consequently, doubt arose concerning their status, for there was reason to suspect that they were not priests at all but Israelites descended from Barzillai, since there was also an Israelite family known as the descendants of Barzillai. Therefore, they were disqualified from the priesthood. In particular, this uncertainty created an additional concern that they were halalim—persons disqualified from the priesthood through improper priestly unions—because, owing to their uncertain status, they themselves had not refrained from marrying women forbidden to priests. This too is included in the words “they were disqualified,” for they had already become defiled with respect to the priesthood by marrying disqualified women. This accounts for the halalim counted among the ten genealogical classes.
text.1_Chapter, 62_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the Tirshatha said”—The question now arose whether they were permitted to eat from the sacred offerings. “And the Tirshatha said”—this was Nehemiah, as it is written, “And Nehemiah, who was the Tirshatha, said” [Nehemiah 8:9]—that they should not eat until there would be Urim and Thummim and the doubt could be resolved by consulting them. I have already explained in my commentary on the Aramaic Targum that, had they then been worthy, the Divine Presence would have returned to them in the Second Temple and they would have possessed the Urim and Thummim. At the time of their ascent, they still hoped that this would occur.
text.1_Chapter, 63_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(64) The total number does not agree with the sum of the individual figures.
text.1_Chapter, 63_Verse, 1_Comment: “The entire congregation together”—The individual figures fall short of the total by thirteen thousand; see Rashi. Apparently, the individual enumeration did not include everyone who came, but only those who first arrived from Babylon. Even in Nehemiah, which also includes those who came from the land of the Chaldeans [as I explained on verse 1], not everyone was counted individually, because additional people arrived every day who are not mentioned in the enumeration here. Those who joined families from which people had already arrived were added to the individual family totals in Nehemiah. New families, however, or individuals who came from cities not previously represented, were not mentioned individually at all. Nevertheless, they were included in the general count, so that after all the groups had assembled, their number was forty-two thousand, etc. Here, the descendants of Magbish number one hundred and fifty-six, whereas Nehemiah does not mention them. It must therefore be that Nehemiah included them within one of the families whose number is greater there. For example, the descendants of Azgad number one thousand more there. It may be that all the people of the city of Magbish belonged to the family of Azgad: here they were counted according to their city, while there they were counted according to their family. This may also explain why the descendants of Arah and the descendants of Zattu are each fewer by one hundred in Nehemiah than in the first count. It may be that one hundred descendants of Arah and one hundred descendants of Zattu lived in the city of Senaah and were counted there among the people of their city. This would explain why Nehemiah adds three hundred to the descendants of Senaah, without requiring the strained explanation that some of them returned to Babylon.
text.1_Chapter, 68_Verse, 0_Comment: “And some of the heads of the ancestral houses”—There are discrepancies between the figures mentioned here and those mentioned in Nehemiah, chapter 7; they will be explained there.
text.1_Chapter, 69_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they settled”—Upon arriving, they first occupied themselves with working the land in order to secure food. They sowed fields and planted vineyards so that the land would produce crops and they would not suffer the disgrace of hunger. Furthermore, because they had not been granted permission to rebuild the wall, they did not settle in Jerusalem. Instead, they dispersed among their cities, each person settling in another city where his ancestors had lived in earlier times. The priests and Levites settled in the forty-eight Levitical cities, while the Israelites settled in the cities of Israel.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the month arrived”—This means “the month came.” It is expressed in the simple conjugation to indicate that when the month had barely arrived, they had already assembled, for they had come several days beforehand in order to be there for Rosh Hashanah and the festivals that followed it.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they built it in order to offer burnt offerings upon it”—Apparently, Scripture is precise in indicating that they offered only burnt offerings and no other sacrifices, as is also evident from the verses [3–6]. This supports the opinion of Raavad in chapter 6 of the Laws of the Temple, that the Temple’s sanctity ceased at the time of its destruction, as well as the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in chapter 14 of Zevahim that, even at a public altar, the community was permitted to offer only the Passover offerings and obligatory offerings whose times were fixed and whose type could also be brought as an individual voluntary offering—that is, the daily offerings and the burnt offerings sacrificed on the festival, since an individual may also voluntarily offer a burnt offering. Sin offerings and guilt offerings, however—such as the festival goats—were not offered upon a great public altar. Likewise, on Yom Kippur they offered neither the goats nor the bulls, as Tosafot explain. Individual obligatory offerings were certainly not offered, nor were meal offerings, since meal offerings were not permitted upon an altar outside the Temple. The verses can therefore be understood literally: they offered burnt offerings alone.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(3–6) What does the reason given—“for fear was upon them because of the peoples of the lands”—explain? Why does Scripture repeatedly state that they offered burnt offerings, implying that they did not offer the additional sin offerings required on Rosh Chodesh and the festivals, and why did they not offer them?
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: “And they set the altar upon its foundations”—As our Sages said, three prophets came up with them from the exile, one of whom testified concerning the location of the altar. The statement “for fear was upon them because of the peoples of the lands” explains why they waited until the entire people had assembled. They had not built the altar before then because they feared that the peoples of the lands would stop them while they were still few in number.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the daily burnt offerings in their prescribed number”—fourteen lambs each day; “according to the ordinance required for each day”—the bulls of the festival, whose number decreased from day to day.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For Ezra was delayed on the journey for four months, and they had to wait for the messenger to travel there and return. It is also evident that they did not offer the lambs of Shavuot. Although voluntary peace offerings could be brought, they were not comparable: the Shavuot lambs were offerings of the most sacred order, whereas ordinary peace offerings were offerings of lesser sanctity, as Tosafot explain. According to the opinion that sacrifices may be offered even when the Temple is not standing, however, one must interpret the word “burnt offerings” as not being exclusive.
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(7) Why does Scripture say, “in accordance with the authorization granted to them by Cyrus,” which appears to be superfluous?
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: “In accordance with the authorization of Cyrus”—The cedars of Lebanon belonged to the king, and they could not take timber from there without the king’s permission, as is evident in Nehemiah [2:8]. They sent people to bring timber from there, not to purchase it with money, because Cyrus’s written decree stated, “Let the expenses be paid from the royal treasury,” as explained below [Ezra 6:4]. Since he had ordered that the cost of construction be borne at his expense, they were permitted to take the timber in accordance with the authorization that Cyrus had granted them.
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(8–9) Why does Scripture say twice, “to supervise”—first, “to supervise the work of the House of Hashem,” and then, “to supervise those performing the work”? At first, it appears that all the Levites were appointed over this task.
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: “Who had come from captivity to Jerusalem, to supervise”—that is, to sing at the time the foundation was laid, as stated in verse 10.
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “The descendants of Judah”—This is stated to distinguish him from another Kadmiel among the descendants of Henadad, as mentioned in Nehemiah 10:10. “To supervise”—here it means to oversee those performing the work, whereas all the Levites participated in directing the song, as stated in the preceding verse.
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “Clothed”—in garments of honor; thus Rashi explains it. This accords with the opinion of Maimonides in chapter 8 of the Laws of the Temple Vessels, that priests were not permitted to wear the priestly garments except while performing the service. According to Raavad’s view there, however, it may be explained that they were clothed in the priestly garments. Even according to Maimonides, it may be said that they wore the priestly garments for the service of the daily offering and for turning one of its limbs with a hook; they were then permitted to continue wearing them throughout the day, as I wrote in my work Artzot HaChaim [section 18]. The priests ordinarily sounded the trumpets only on the festivals, as Maimonides states [Laws of the Temple Vessels, chapter 3]. On this occasion, however, it was a temporary ruling, for they regarded the day as a festival because of their great joy. “According to the direction of David”—with the songs and praises composed by David.
text.2_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they responded with praise and thanksgiving”—Praise refers to extolling the Creator, whereas thanksgiving is offered for the good He has bestowed. Scripture explains that in their praise they proclaimed, “For He is good,” meaning that this praise is fitting because He is intrinsically good; and in their thanksgiving they proclaimed, “For His kindness toward Israel endures forever.” “And the people raised a great shout in praise of Hashem”—but not in thanksgiving, because many of them were weeping, as the following verse relates.
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(12–13) Why does Scripture say that the sound of the joyful shouting could not be distinguished because the people were shouting so loudly? This appears self-contradictory.
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: “Who had seen”—The word “seen” also applies to what follows, while the words “with their own eyes” also apply to what precedes. The meaning is: Those who had seen the First Temple [with their own eyes], and now saw the foundation of this Temple with their own eyes, were weeping, as it is written [Haggai 2], “Who among you remains who saw this House in its former glory, and how do you see it now?” “But many shouted aloud”—This may be explained according to Maimonides’ statement in chapter 1 of the Laws of Terumot regarding why the sanctity established by Joshua ceased, whereas the sanctity established by Ezra did not cease. Joshua’s sanctification was accomplished through conquest; therefore, when the Land was conquered by enemies, the conquest was nullified and its sanctity ceased. Ezra’s sanctification, however, was established through possession and consequently did not cease. Many wept because they saw that the people were building with Cyrus’s permission and in accordance with his decree, which restricted the dimensions and character of the building, as explained below [chapter 6]. Had they been worthy, a miracle would have occurred for them in Ezra’s days as it had in the days of Joshua son of Nun, as our Sages stated [Berakhot 4a]; over this they wept. Many others, however, rejoiced precisely because the new sanctification would thereby endure forever and never cease. This is the meaning of the verse:
text.2_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shouting”—because of the sound of the people’s weeping. The very circumstance over which some wept—that they were building under Cyrus’s authority—was itself the reason many who understood its benefit rejoiced. The multitude did not understand this; they simply raised a great shout. This is the homiletical interpretation. According to the plain meaning, neither of the two sounds—the sound of joy or the sound of weeping—could be distinguished because of the blasts of the trumpets, which could be heard from afar and drowned out all the other sounds.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(2–3) Why did they not accept the Samaritans, who wished to worship Hashem? And what is meant by the answer, “We alone shall build, as Cyrus commanded us”? Did Cyrus command them not to allow the nations to assist in the construction?
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: “Let us build with you, for like you we seek your God”—The Samaritans worshiped God together with other deities, as it is written, “They feared Hashem, while worshiping their own gods.” They thought that Israel also worshiped in this manner. Therefore, they said, “Like you, we seek your God,” for they called Him “the God of gods.” Accordingly, they added, “And to Him we have been sacrificing,” meaning that they regarded Him as the supreme God, exalted above all other gods.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then the people of the land”—As a result, the people of the land—the Samaritans—became their adversaries and devised schemes to halt the construction. At times, they weakened their hands, meaning that they induced lethargy among them so that they would make no effort toward the construction. At other times, they frightened them away from building by casting fear upon them. Still other times, they hired counselors against them to frustrate the construction. This continued throughout all the days of Cyrus, during whose reign construction was halted, until the reign of Darius, when they resumed building. Scripture now explains:
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “And in the reign of Ahasuerus, they wrote an accusation”—At that time, they weakened their hands and frightened them by means of the accusation they had written against them.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(7–11) At first Scripture says that the writers were Bishlam, Mithredath, and Tabeel; afterward, it says that they were Rehum the counselor and Shimshai; and then it says that they also included the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, and others. Finally, it again says, “This is a copy of the letter,” etc., “Your servants, the people beyond the River.” Who, then, actually wrote the letter? And why does Scripture repeat that the letter was written in Aramaic, after already stating, “The text of the document was written in Aramaic”?
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: “And in the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam wrote”—At that time, they hired counselors against them to frustrate the construction, as we shall explain. Although there are various opinions concerning the Persian kings and their names, this Artaxerxes must have been Cyrus, as Rashi explains, since construction was halted during Cyrus’s reign. We must therefore say that “Artaxerxes” was an honorific title used for the Persian kings. According to the opinion that Artaxerxes was the name of a different king, we must say that construction was not halted until after Cyrus’s death, and that this Artaxerxes was a king who reigned after Cyrus. In any event, we must say that construction was suspended for fourteen years—the two weeks mentioned in Daniel [9:25], according to my interpretation. Before explaining the following passage, I shall present an introduction, for several matters are extremely perplexing. First, Cyrus himself had issued the decree authorizing the Temple’s construction and had said that Hashem had charged him to build Him a House. How, then, could he have reversed his decree and halted the construction only a short time later? We know that under the laws of Persia and Media, any document written in the king’s name could not be revoked by the king under any circumstances. This is evident from the account of Daniel [Daniel 6] and from that of Ahasuerus, who could not revoke the written decree even though it had been issued in error, as we explained in our commentary on the Book of Esther. Second, they wrote that the Jews were building and fortifying the walls of Jerusalem. This was entirely false, for the Jews were building only the Temple. The wall was not built until the days of Artaxerxes, who granted special permission for it. Moreover, how could the construction of the Temple enable a rebellion when they had no fortified city in which to take refuge? The Temple was being built from wood and stone and could easily have been burned if they rebelled against the king’s command, as will be explained in chapter 6. How, then, did the king heed these lies, and how did they dare to speak falsely? These questions illuminate the meaning of the verses. In truth, an elaborate deception was carried out. Through monetary bribes, the adversaries of Judah hired counselors, and their deceit succeeded. They knew that it was impossible to revoke the decree authorizing the Temple’s construction, because under the laws of Persia and Media, a document written in the king’s name could not be rescinded. They also knew that they could not accuse the Jews of rebellion merely for building the House of God, since Jerusalem’s wall remained breached. Yet they were afraid to write falsely to the king that the Jews had violated his command and, instead of building the Temple, were rebuilding the city wall, lest the king discover their falsehood and hold them liable with their lives. They therefore devised the following plan. Because the Persian Empire was vast and extensive, and the various peoples under its rule each spoke their own language, the law permitted anyone wishing to write to the king to write in his own language and script, as it is written, “that every man should rule in his own house and speak the language of his own people.” In each province, two royal officials were appointed to receive letters written in the language of that province, translate them into the Persian language and script, and send them to the king. Likewise, the king’s reply would arrive in Persian language and script to these two translators. They would translate it into the language of the province and deliver the translated response to the original writers. The officials appointed over the province of Syria were Rehum the counselor, who translated from one language into another, and Shimshai the scribe, who converted the writing into Persian script. The language and script used in Syria were Aramaic. Therefore, the three men who composed the accusation—Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their associates, meaning their companions and assistants—wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The text of the document—that is, the document that had to be translated, with the translation made to correspond precisely to the original—was written in Aramaic and translated in Aramaic; that is, it was in Aramaic script and the Aramaic language. They delivered this letter, prepared for the king, to Rehum the counselor and Shimshai the scribe so that they could translate it into the Persian language and script.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “Rehum”—Rehum the counselor and Shimshai the scribe, who were the translators and were trusted by the king not to falsify their work, now acted deceitfully in preparing their translation. Although the original writers had composed their complaint about the building of the Temple, these officials transformed the document into an accusation concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem. This is the meaning of “they wrote a letter concerning Jerusalem”: they wrote that the Jews were rebuilding and fortifying Jerusalem. Nevertheless, they formulated it so that even if the king learned that the claim was false—that the Jews had built only the Temple and not Jerusalem’s wall—he would be unable to punish either the original writers or the translators, as will be explained in verse 12. “They wrote to King Artaxerxes as follows.” It was one of the king’s regulations that the two officials appointed to translate a letter place their names at its beginning, since the king would hold them accountable if the translation contained any falsification or deception. They would then record the names of the letter’s authors and petitioners, who would be held accountable if the letter itself contained any falsehood; this would also inform the king of the petitioners’ identities. These names were written upon the letter, just as people today sign their names beneath a letter. However, instead of identifying the writers as Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates, the translators wrote that the letter came from all the peoples of the province Beyond the River. The king would therefore take the matter seriously, recognizing that it was not an insignificant complaint but something affecting all the peoples within his realm. Concerning this, they wrote:
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the rest of the nations whom the great and mighty King Sennacherib exiled and settled in the city of Samaria, and the other nations Beyond the River, and the people of Ke‘eneth”—Up to this point, they wrote upon the letter to identify the petitioners, showing that they represented many peoples. It may also be that Bishlam and Mithredath gathered signatures from several cities authorizing them to submit this request in their names.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “This”—From this point begins the actual content of the letter: “This is the interpretation of the letter”—that is, this is its translation—“which they sent to King Artaxerxes: Your servants, the people Beyond the River, and Ke‘eneth.” In quoting the letter, Scripture abbreviated and did not list all of them. It records only the beginning—“Your servants,” etc.—and the end—“Beyond the River, and Ke‘eneth.” Their practice was not to repeat all the names each time, but to record the beginning and the end and write between them the word shelem or gemir, just as we write “etc.,” as you will see in verse 17 and in chapter 7, verse 17. Here, the word shelem or gemir was omitted from the transcription for the sake of brevity.
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(12) How could they say that the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem when this was an obvious falsehood, since they were building only the Temple, in accordance with the king’s authorization?
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: “Let it be known to the king”—Here begins the body of the petition. “The Jews who came up from you”—whom you released and sent away. [This proves that construction was halted during the reign of Cyrus. If this occurred after his reign, one must interpret the phrase as meaning “from your province.”] “Have come to Jerusalem, the rebellious and wicked city; they are building, and they have completed the walls”—Here lay the translators’ deception and falsification, for this wording admits two interpretations. It may be understood as attaching “the rebellious and wicked city” to what precedes: they came to Jerusalem, which is a rebellious and sinful city. The word “building” would then begin a separate statement, meaning that they were constructing a building there—namely, the Temple—and had laid the foundations of the Temple’s walls. That is, they were preparing to build its walls, for “they had already joined together its foundations.” According to this reading, they wrote nothing false: they truly were building the House of Hashem there in accordance with Cyrus’s command. Alternatively, the word “building” may be joined to “the rebellious and wicked city,” meaning that they came to Jerusalem and were rebuilding the rebellious and wicked city. The translators rendered it in this second sense, as though the Jews were rebuilding the city itself. If the king later discovered that this was false, they could not be punished, because the letter’s wording also permitted the first interpretation, which is how we understand it in truth. Nor could the original writers be punished, for they could defend themselves by claiming that they had intended the first interpretation—that the Jews were building the Temple there.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(13–16) Why does Scripture repeat, “Let it be known to the king,” and “We make known to the king”?
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: “Now, let it be known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are completed,” they will no longer pay the various kinds of taxes known as tribute, excise, and toll [because they will rebel against the king], and the royal revenue will suffer damage [or this means the king’s treasury].
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: [They did not mention the salt tax, because salt was supplied to them free of charge.] The royal salt allowance provided for the needs of the king’s palace. This is the meaning of “we eat the king’s salt”: because we are his servants and depend upon his support. Therefore, “the king’s dishonor”—that is, it would be improper for us to witness the king’s disgrace. For this reason, we have sent this letter and informed the king. They explained that what motivated them to report the matter was neither their own benefit nor fear of suffering harm, but solely that they were the king’s faithful servants and did not wish to witness any misfortune befall him.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “That a search be made”—That is, they drew his attention to the fact that he need not believe them solely on the basis of their report, but should search the book of records of his fathers. You will find in the book of records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, and that they have made efforts within it [to rebel] from ancient times. [The word ve’eshtaddur means the same as ve’eshtaddal, as in Daniel 6:15.] It was for this reason that the city was destroyed.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: “We make known”—At first they said, “Let it be known to the king,” meaning that the king would recognize and understand on his own that if the city were rebuilt, he would lose its tax revenues, since its inhabitants had always been accustomed to rebel and throw off the yoke of royal authority. Beyond this, however, “we make known to the king” something he could not know on his own: that if this city is rebuilt, you will have no portion anywhere Beyond the River. For just as this city would cast off the royal yoke, so would all the inhabitants Beyond the River; they would imitate its actions and break free of their restraints.
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(17) The words “Peace, and now” appear to have no explanation.
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: “The reply”—In view of how they presented their claims, it never occurred to the king to investigate whether the allegation itself was true—whether the Jews had violated his command and were rebuilding the city wall without his permission. He assumed that his officials, together with the many peoples who joined them in writing, would not send him such an obvious falsehood. He therefore needed to investigate only whether it was true that the people of Jerusalem had a history of rebelling against kings. He answered accordingly. At the beginning of the letter it was written: “The king sent a message to Rehum the counselor, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates who dwelt in Samaria and elsewhere Beyond the River, [etc., through] Ke‘eneth.” As explained above, the letter would otherwise have had to repeat the names of all the signatories—the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, and the others listed above in verses 9 and 10. To abbreviate, their practice was to write only the beginning—“Rehum the counselor and Shimshai”—followed by shelem, meaning: complete and finish the remaining names through “Ke‘eneth.” It functioned like “etc.” in the texts we write. Similarly, below [7:12] it says, gemir u-kheneth. Here, the word shelem is used instead of gemir, meaning “complete and finish.” I subsequently saw that one scholar had explained it in this manner as well.
text.3_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: “The text”—that is, the translation [which corresponds precisely to the letter from which it was translated] that you sent us was read clearly before me.
text.3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: “And by me”—that is, the command was issued by me, and they searched and found that this city had risen up against kings from ancient times, and that rebellion and incitement [of others to rebel] had taken place within it.
text.3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: “And mighty kings”—Furthermore, there had been mighty kings there who ruled over the entire region Beyond the River, and tribute was paid to them [by the nations]. This also confirmed what they had reported to him: that if the city were rebuilt, he would lose his royal dominion throughout the entire region Beyond the River.
text.3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(21) How could he halt the construction when he himself had granted permission to build, and under Persian law a decree written in the king’s name could not be revoked?
text.3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: “Now”—Issue an order to stop these men, and let this city not be rebuilt until a command is issued by me. Take care not to act negligently in this matter [or inadvertently]. Why should the damage increase, to the detriment of the kings?
text.3_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then, as soon as the interpretation of the copy,” etc.—The king’s decree did not mention halting the construction of the Temple, but only the rebuilding of the city. However, his words, “Stop these men, and let this city not be rebuilt,” could be interpreted as stating two separate commands: first, “Stop these men” from building the Temple—for since they were not actually rebuilding the city, there was no occasion to stop them from doing so—and second, “Let this city not be rebuilt,” an additional command forbidding the city’s reconstruction. This interpretation would have been correct had the letter sent to the king been an accusation concerning the building of the Temple, for the king’s reply would then have meant that they were to stop the Jews from building the Temple. In truth, however, the translators had transformed the accusation into one concerning the rebuilding of the city. Accordingly, the king’s words, “Stop these men,” meant to stop them from rebuilding the city, and “Let this city not be rebuilt” explained what they were to stop them from doing. Construction of the Temple remained permitted under the king’s original decree, which could not be revoked. But because Rehum and Shimshai the scribe were the translators, they now claimed that the accusation had concerned the building of the Temple. They interpreted “the interpretation of the copy”—that is, their rendering of the translated copy of the king’s letter, which had likewise arrived in Persian and which they translated and interpreted—as meaning that the king intended to halt construction of the Temple. Since the interpretation of the letter was in their hands, they hurried to Jerusalem, to the Jews, and stopped them by force and military power.
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they prophesied”—In the second year of Darius, the seventy-year period from the destruction of Jerusalem was completed [as explained above on 1:1 and in Daniel 9:2]. Haggai and Zechariah [“son of Iddo” means his grandson] then prophesied in the name of Hashem that the time to build had arrived, and the people began construction in reliance upon the prophets and their assurance.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(3–4) Why did they ask who had granted permission to build, when there had been a second decree prohibiting construction? And what is meant by, “Then we told them the names of the men”? This statement appears entirely unexplained.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: “At that time”—This was through Hashem’s Providence, for their adversaries did not come against them. Their adversaries would have forcibly obstructed them, as they had the first time and as they later sought to fight them over the construction of the wall. Instead, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, came. He was not an adversary of the Jews; he merely asked who had authorized them to build this Temple, because Cyrus’s authorization had been forgotten by that time.
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then”—They questioned the builders, and the builders related: “We answered them in these words, stating the names of the men who were constructing this building.” The builders explained: We answered Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai by saying that we were not building on our own authority; rather, Zerubbabel and the High Priest were the true builders, since we were building under their command. Zerubbabel had been appointed governor by the king. Undoubtedly, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, and his associates then spoke with Zerubbabel, and they replied to them in the terms recorded in Tattenai’s letter to the king beginning with verse 11.
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the eye”—The governor of the province Beyond the River had the power to suspend construction until Darius’s reply arrived. It was therefore through the Providence of Hashem’s watchful eye that they did not halt construction in the meantime, “until the matter should go before Darius”—meaning that they were told not to stop the builders until the matter had been sent to Darius to learn his decision. “And then they would return a written response concerning the matter”—Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, and his colleagues would then return with a copy of whatever answer the king gave.
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(6–7) Why does Scripture repeat, “a copy of the letter,” “they sent a report to him,” and “in it was written as follows”?
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: “A copy”—This is the wording that appeared on the outside of the letter they sent to Darius. [As explained above, the sender’s identity and signature were written on the outside.] The following was written there: “A copy of the letter”—that is, a copy of the letter sent by Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the nation called the Apharsachites who were Beyond the River, to King Darius. “They sent him a report”—up to this point was written on the outside. The meaning of “they sent him a report” is that this letter contained neither a request nor an accusation, but merely an inquiry asking the king to issue a ruling and response. All this appeared on the outside. “And thus was written within it”—the following was written inside it. From this point, Scripture transcribes the letter’s internal contents. Its wording was: “To King Darius, all peace.” This indicated that the letter contained no accusation or hostile matter.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(8–17) Did they not know that a decree had been issued to halt construction? Why, then, did they write this entire lengthy account?
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: “Let it be known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the House of the great God, and it is being built with marble, while timber is being laid within the walls.” In this statement, they spoke in the Jews’ favor by explaining that they were not constructing a strong fortress, since they were placing timber within the walls, which could easily be destroyed by fire and was unsuitable for defensive purposes. [For this reason, Cyrus commanded that every fourth course be constructed of timber, as stated below in 6:4.] “And this work is being performed rapidly and is prospering in their hands.” With this as well, they advocated on the Jews’ behalf, explaining that the surrounding peoples were not interfering with the work because it presented no danger of rebellion and contained nothing harmful to the king or the other peoples.
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then we questioned these elders: Who granted them permission for this? We also asked their names, so that we could inform you of the names of the men who stood at their head.” This too was intended in their favor, for it showed that the governor stood at their head, and he would not act without authorization. Their claim that they possessed explicit permission was therefore undoubtedly true.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “And thus they answered us, saying”—First, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth,” and this House is being built for His great name. Second, this House possesses an established claim by virtue of its antiquity, for “it was built many years ago.” Third, it possesses an established claim by virtue of the greatness of its builder, who was “a great and powerful king.”
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: “However”—Fourth, its destruction had been caused by their sins, and those sins had already been atoned for through the exile. Fifth, in the first year of Cyrus, the appointed term of their affliction and exile came to an end. Cyrus then issued the decree to rebuild this House, and they were therefore building with royal authorization.
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “Moreover”—The proof is that Cyrus brought out the Temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the Sanctuary and carried to the temple in Babylon. Because Belshazzar made use of these vessels, he was killed and the kingdom was transferred to Persia. Cyrus consequently restored the vessels and gave them to Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed governor. Two pieces of evidence therefore confirm their account: the vessels were in their possession, and Sheshbazzar was a governor formally appointed by the king. Cyrus had commanded him to build, and he was the one carrying out the construction. A governor who served as the king’s official would not undertake such a project without authorization. Therefore, if it pleases the king, let him investigate and search whether such a decree from Cyrus can be found, and let him send us his decision concerning this matter.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment:
The question:
(1–2) How can Scripture say that they searched in the archive house in Babylon but found the document in Media?
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: “Then King Darius issued a command, and they searched in the archive house where the records were stored in Babylon. And a single scroll was found in a chest in the fortress located in the province of Media, and the following was written in it as a memorandum.” It appears that the royal capital was originally in Babylon, and all the records of the king’s decrees were kept there. The letter Cyrus had issued concerning the construction—whose wording began, “Hashem has given me all the kingdoms of the earth,” as stated at the beginning of the book—was likewise kept in Babylon. In the days of Ahasuerus, however, the royal throne was transferred from Babylon to Shushan, as it is written, “upon his royal throne, which was in Shushan the fortress,” as I explained in my commentary there. At that time, this letter was lost. [It is possible that Haman the Agagite, who was viceroy, destroyed this document because it favored the Jews.] It was therefore not found in Babylon. Through Hashem’s Providence, however, a small scroll was found in the royal fortress, which was now in Media, containing a memorandum of this decree. [This document remained in Media, just as the book of chronicles and records was kept there, as I explained in my commentary on the Book of Esther; that book was not under Haman’s control.] There the decree had been recorded briefly as a memorandum.
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: “In the first year of King Cyrus, the king issued a decree”—First, “Let the House of God in Jerusalem be rebuilt,” thereby granting permission to rebuild the Temple. Second, it was to be a place where sacrifices would be offered. Third, “and let its foundations be strongly laid,” so that the Temple’s foundations would be strong enough to support the structure. Fourth, he prescribed the Temple’s dimensions. This too occurred through Divine Providence, for he did not alter its proper dimensions, and they would otherwise have been unable to build it in accordance with what is written: “All this was given in writing from the hand of Hashem, who granted me understanding.” Fifth—
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “Three courses of marble and one course of new timber”—According to our Sages, this was so that if they rebelled, he could burn the Temple with fire. Sixth, the expenses of the construction were to be paid from the royal treasury. Seventh, he brought out the vessels of Hashem and delivered them into their hands.
text.5_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “Now”—You, Tattenai, etc., “keep away from there.” Remain distant from this construction and do not hinder those performing the work, since they possess authorization from Cyrus, in accordance with the law of Persia and Media, which may not be revoked. Therefore, “leave the work on this House of God alone.” You must not interfere in the matter, for the responsibility rests upon the governor of the Jews and the Jewish elders to rebuild it upon its site. All this followed from Cyrus’s original decree, which did not command the officials to assist them with the construction, but only forbade them from interrupting their work: the Jews themselves were to build. Under this decree, you are required to remain at a distance—neither assisting them nor hindering the work. However—
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “And by me a decree is issued”—I hereby issue a new decree in addition to Cyrus’s decree. Under Cyrus’s decree, it was sufficient for you to remain distant and refrain from acting. Under my decree, however, it is not enough that you refrain from hindering the work; you are also obligated to take positive action to assist it. This is the meaning of “what you shall do for these Jewish elders”: you must act together with them and assist them “in rebuilding this House of God.” I further command that “from the king’s possessions, from the tribute collected in the province Beyond the River, the expenses shall promptly be paid” to them. [Cyrus’s decree stated that the expenses were to come from the royal treasury, but they were not supplied promptly. I command that they be paid from the tribute collected Beyond the River and that they be supplied immediately.] “So that they should not be hindered”—so that a lack of funds would not cause them to cease their work.
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment:
The questions:
(9–12) At first, he told them to “keep away from there,” implying that they should not intervene at all; afterward, he said, “what you shall do for these Jewish elders,” requiring them to assist with the construction. And why does he repeat the phrase “and by me a decree is issued” three times?
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: “And whatever they require”—He added further to Cyrus’s decree: the expenses of the sacrifices and the necessities of the Temple service were also to be supplied to them, something not mentioned in the earlier decree. That is, whatever they might require—young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil—was to be given to them daily, without delay, according to the instructions of the priests in Jerusalem, so that they might offer sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the lives of the king and his sons.
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “And by me a decree is issued”—This decree too comes from me [for it was not included in Cyrus’s original decree]: whoever alters this command shall have a beam torn from his house, and from it a gallows shall be made upon which he will be hanged at the entrance to his house; his house shall then be reduced to a dunghill.
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: “And may the God”—However, if any king or nation [over whom I have no authority] should seek to destroy this House, may Hashem who dwells there destroy him. “I, Darius”—that is, in addition to Cyrus’s decree that the Temple be built, I have issued a decree that it be carried out promptly. This means both that the Temple should be built quickly and that Tattenai and his associates should communicate the decree without delay. Therefore, Scripture says, “Then”—that is, in exact accordance with what Darius had sent, they carried out his decree promptly, as he had commanded.
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the Jewish elders—and they completed it by the command of the God of Israel,” etc.—That is, Divine Providence was clothed in natural events: it was by the command of the God of Israel, and thus providential, but it was not an open miracle. Rather, it occurred through the command of the kings, for Hashem placed this intention in their hearts. As our Sages said, Israel was worthy that a miracle be performed for them in the days of Ezra as it had been in the days of Joshua son of Nun, but sin prevented it. Regarding the words “Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes,” according to our Sages in Rosh Hashanah, these are different names of one person. Rashi likewise explains that Artaxerxes is Darius and was called by that name as a royal title. Similarly, on the verse above [4:7], “And in the days of Artaxerxes,” Rashi explains that this refers to Cyrus, for such is the opinion of our Sages. However, Rabbi Zerahiah HaLevi writes in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: “This is the conclusion that emerges according to the interpretation of the Sages; but the correct explanation according to the plain meaning is that the statement ‘by the command of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes’ refers to three kings: Cyrus, who began the process; Darius, who completed the building of the Temple; and immediately afterward Artaxerxes, who built the walls of Jerusalem.” Many different systems and opinions have been proposed concerning the number and names of the Persian kings, and nothing in this matter is certain.
text.5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they completed it”—The construction was completed on the third of Adar, in the sixth year of Darius’s reign. Thus, the construction lasted four years and six months [see Haggai 1:15].
text.5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they celebrated the dedication of this House with joy”—The earlier commentators have already explained the expression “this House.” Had they been worthy at that time, the appointed time of the future redemption would have arrived, and immediately after the construction of this Temple, the Temple from heaven—the future Sanctuary seen by Ezekiel—would have descended, and they would have begun the second dedication described in Ezekiel. For the time being, however, they celebrated the dedication of this House, the word “this” indicating the expectation of the dedication of another House. Ezekiel’s dedication is to begin on the twenty-third of Adar, as explained there. They therefore extended their dedication until the twenty-third of Adar, a period of twenty-one days. Had they been worthy, the dedication of the final Temple, to be built by Heaven, would have begun immediately afterward. Since Purim, a time of feasting and rejoicing, occurred during these days, Scripture emphasizes that their principal joy concerned the dedication, which exceeded even the joy of Purim.
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they offered”—These communal goat sin offerings were not brought in accordance with the ordinary law, but as a temporary ruling directed by the prophets, as the Gemara concludes in Horayot and Temurah.
text.5_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they appointed the priests according to their divisions”—The priests were divided into twenty-four watches, each serving during a different week. Each watch was further divided into seven ancestral houses, each serving on a different day. The particular service each priest performed, however, was assigned by lot. The Levites were divided even more specifically: the heads of the ancestral houses assigned each individual a particular task, as explained by Maimonides [Laws of the Temple Vessels, chapter 3, law 10]; see the Kesef Mishneh there. Therefore, regarding the Levites Scripture says, “according to their assignments,” because they were divided more specifically than the priests, each man being designated for his particular service.
text.5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: “For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together”—In contrast to what Ezra wrote in II Chronicles [29:34], that “the Levites were more upright of heart in sanctifying themselves than the priests,” Scripture says that now they purified themselves equally. Lest one think that some priests and Levites nevertheless remained impure, it adds, “all of them were pure.” “For all the exiles”—The Levites slaughtered the Passover offerings on behalf of the people, as is likewise stated in II Chronicles [30:16; 35:6, 10–11]. Scripture relates to their credit that they gave precedence to the Passover offerings of the Israelites before those of the priests, who were diligent in performing the commandments, and to the priests’ offerings before their own.
text.5_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: “And all who had separated themselves”—These were the converts, as stated in Kiddushin 70a.
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: “The king of Assyria”—This refers to the king of Persia, who also ruled over Assyria. The officials and governors stationed there, who governed the entire region Beyond the River, had always been adversaries of Israel. Now, however, even the kingdom of Assyria—meaning all the royal officials—favored them and strengthened their hands. This is similar to the expression “the king of Greece” in Daniel [8:21], which means the kingdom of Greece.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “Zechariah, son of Iddo”—In Chronicles, six additional generations are listed; here, their genealogy is abbreviated.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “This Ezra”—Simeon the Righteous, one of the last surviving members of the Great Assembly, said: “The world stands upon three things: upon the Torah, upon the Temple service, and upon acts of lovingkindness.” During the period of the Great Assembly, these three pillars were firmly established by three distinguished men. Through Zerubbabel and Joshua the High Priest, the Temple was built and the pillar of the Temple service was established. After them came Ezra to establish the pillar of Torah. After him came Nehemiah, who rebuilt the city walls and attended to the affairs of government, thereby strengthening the pillar of lovingkindness, as will be explained in his book. This is the meaning of the statement that “he went up” because “he was a skilled scribe in the Torah of Hashem”: he went up to establish the pillar of Torah. This was what he requested from the king, and the king granted it to him, as stated from verse 25 onward. For this reason, the hand of God was favorably upon him through His particular Providence, so that the Torah would not be forgotten from Israel.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “It was the seventh year”—According to our Sages in Rosh Hashanah, who held that the years of his reign were counted from Nisan, the earlier phrase “in the seventh year” may mean that on that day he entered his seventh year, while here “the seventh year” refers to a point in the middle of that year. According to the plain meaning, however, it may be said that kings individually counted the years of their reign from the date of their accession. He became king on the second day of the fifth month, and when they arrived in Jerusalem on that same date, the seventh year of his reign ended, for on the following day they began counting the eighth year.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “The beginning of the journey”—This was when the initial stage of their ascent began. According to Ibn Ezra, the word yesod is related to counsel and deliberation, meaning that at that time they resolved to make the journey, for they did not depart from the River Ahava until the twelfth day of the month [below, 8:31].
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “For Ezra”—Scripture explains the statement that he arrived “because the good hand of his God was upon him.” That is, he was accompanied by particular Divine Providence, which protected him on the journey and brought him to his destination. This was in the merit of the Torah [as explained above on verse 6], for he had prepared his heart for three things: first, “to expound the Torah of Hashem”—he personally studied and investigated its meaning; second, “and to practice it”—for study is not the essential thing, but practice; and third, “and to teach in Israel”—to teach others both statute and ordinance. It may be that “statute” includes the interpretations of the Oral Torah, which are called “the statutes of Hashem,” as I have written frequently in HaTorah VeHaMitzvah.
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “And this is a copy of the document”—That is, the king gave him the decree in the Persian script and language, and it was translated into Aramaic, the language spoken in the province of Syria, by the royal officials appointed for this purpose, who attested that the translation corresponded precisely to the original document. This is the meaning of the word nishtavan, as explained above. “A scribe of the words of the commandments”—Scripture explains why he was called a scribe. It was not because he practiced scribal work as his occupation, but because he counted and recorded the words of Hashem’s commandments. He counted the letters of the Torah and established safeguards for the Masoretic text. He likewise established safeguards in the transmission of the other books of Scripture, purifying them of every corruption. He also recorded the transmitted teachings of the Oral Torah, which are included in the term “statutes,” as explained above. “Concerning Israel”—This phrase apparently refers back to what precedes: “which the king granted to Ezra concerning Israel”—that is, for the sake of Israel and for their needs.
text.6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: “Artaxerxes”—This begins the text of the letter, for kings customarily signed their names at the beginning of their letters. “Complete, and so forth”—I have already explained that the decree mentioned all the nations Beyond the River. It read: “To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, the Dinaites and the Apharsachites,” and continued by listing them as above [4:9–10], ending with “and the rest of those Beyond the River, and so forth.” The decree was also addressed to them so that they would strengthen Ezra’s hand, as stated in verse 21. For the sake of brevity, Scripture records only the beginning, “To Ezra the priest,” and the end, “and so forth,” placing the word gemir between them. This is equivalent to “etc.” Above [4:17], the word shelem is used with the same meaning as “and so forth.”
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: “By me a decree is issued”—In the original decree granting the exiles permission to go to Jerusalem, Cyrus explained that the purpose of their journey was to build the House of Hashem there. Once the Temple’s construction had been completed, that decree had fulfilled its purpose. From that point onward, the exiles were no longer permitted to leave the land of their captivity without special authorization. Therefore, the king now granted new permission: any member of Israel who freely chose to depart with Ezra was authorized to go.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “Inasmuch as”—Scripture explains the reason for this authorization: because you are an emissary of the king and his seven counselors for two purposes. First, “to inquire concerning the Jews,” which was to be done in Jerusalem, according to the law of your God that is in your hand. That is, you were to oversee their religious affairs, teach them the law, strengthen its observance, and spread the light of Torah and the fear of Hashem among them. Therefore, anyone who wished to attach himself to you and accompany you in order to study Torah and faith in the Holy City was authorized to go.
text.6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “And to bring”—Second, you are an emissary charged with transporting a great quantity of silver and gold there, and you require many men to protect you from robbers along the journey. Scripture explains that he was to transport three kinds of funds: first, the contributions donated by the king and his counselors.
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Second, “all the silver and gold that you shall find”—whatever the gentiles throughout the province would contribute; and third, whatever Israel would contribute, as indicated by the words “together with the voluntary offering,” etc. This required additional protection.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: “Therefore”—He now instructed Ezra what to do with the money he would bring as a donation: he was to purchase sacrifices promptly and offer them upon the altar. With any silver and gold that remained, he could do whatever the law permitted to be done with surplus funds, as enumerated by Maimonides in the Laws of Shekalim. The vessels, however, were not to be used for any other purpose; they were to remain sacred service vessels and be delivered intact to the House of God for the needs of the Temple service.
text.6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: “And whatever else”—Whatever else is needed for the House of God and that you must provide shall be supplied from the royal treasury. I issue a command to all the treasurers Beyond the River that whatever Ezra requests be provided promptly and without delay, up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred kors of wheat, etc. “And salt without limit”—salt was to be supplied without a fixed limit [as explained above on 4:14], because the king had salt available to him free of charge.
text.6_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: “Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven shall be carried out under seal”—[The word adrazda means “a seal” in Arabic.] “For the House of the God of heaven”—He further commanded that a seal be made bearing the inscription that it was the seal of the House of God. Every directive issued from the House of Hashem would be stamped with this seal and would have the legal force of a command issued by the God of heaven, just as a document sealed with the king’s signet has the force of the king’s own command. This bestowed great honor upon the House of God: it could issue commands under Hashem’s seal, and this seal possessed authority and power from the king. “Why should”—This gives the reason for all his commands: so that God would not become angry with his kingdom if they failed to take proper care regarding the service of His House.
text.6_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: “And we make known to you”—That is, he informed the treasurers responsible for collecting taxes that they had no authority to collect any tax from those who served in the Temple.
text.6_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: “And you, Ezra”—He further granted Ezra the authority to appoint judges who would judge the people according to Torah law. He said “magistrates and judges”: “magistrates” refers to expert judges, while “judges” refers to those who were not experts—namely, a court of three ordinary persons, among whom there must be at least one who is learned. Corresponding to the magistrates, he said, “all who know the laws of your God,” meaning experts; and corresponding to the judges, he said, “and whoever does not know, you shall teach,” meaning that they would teach such a judge some of the relevant laws.
text.6_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: “And whoever”—He also granted the judges authority to compel observance of both the law of God and the law of the king. They were empowered to punish anyone who violated either Hashem’s law or the king’s law, whether by death or by eradication—the uprooting of the offender’s entire family—and so forth. Thus, the authority to impose punishments was likewise placed in their hands.
