text.6_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: “Blessed is Hashem”—Ezra gives thanks to Hashem, both for what He did to glorify the House of Hashem by placing it in the king’s heart to contribute to the House of God, and for what He did for Ezra personally by granting him the authority to strengthen the law and appoint judges. Concerning this he says, “And He extended kindness to me.”
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “The heads of their ancestral houses and their genealogy”—Each head of an ancestral house possessed a genealogical record tracing his lineage back to the tribes, while all those belonging to that ancestral house possessed records establishing their descent from it. Thus, among the descendants of Shecaniah, of the descendants of Parosh, their genealogical records traced their lineage as far as Zechariah, while Zechariah possessed a genealogical record tracing his own ancestry further back. The same was true of all the others.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: “The last ones”—No one from this family remained outside the Land. On the first occasion [2:13], 666 of them had departed, and those leaving now were the last members of this family who had remained behind.
text.7_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “To the river”—the river that flows into the River Ahava, for the first river had no particular name.
text.7_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: “For Eliezer”—I sent them on a mission [the preposition lamed is used in place of the direct-object marker et, as in “he killed Abner”]. “Leading men”—leaders of the people. “Men of understanding”—wise men.
text.7_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: “And I commissioned them”—I sent them on a mission to speak to Iddo. [Whenever a command concerning a third party is expressed, it is constructed with the word al, as in, “Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him.”] “At the place Casiphia”—because there was also a province called Casiphia. “To Iddo and his brethren, the Temple servants”—they had been appointed there by the king as officials over that place.
text.7_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: “A man of understanding”—this was Sherebiah. Scripture explains that this Sherebiah, whom they brought together with his sons and brothers, was one of a group of eighteen.
text.7_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: “And from the Temple servants”—These were the Gibeonites whom David assigned to the Temple service, for originally they had been hewers of wood for the congregation, as stated in Joshua [9:27].
text.7_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: “For us and for our children”—He mentioned first those whose rescue was primary, and then added a request even for the secondary dependents. This is the manner of one who prays: he begins by asking for little and then adds to his request, as it is written, “Who can discern errors? Cleanse me from hidden faults,” and as explained in the Midrash.
text.7_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: “For I was ashamed”—Although it would have been proper not to rely upon a miracle—for even though those engaged in performing a commandment are not harmed, the rule is different where danger is common—and they therefore should have requested soldiers and horsemen, Ezra says that they were ashamed to make such a request. They had declared that Hashem’s particular Providence always accompanied them miraculously; therefore, they sought this protection from God. “And He granted our entreaty”—Ibn Ezra explains that Hashem informed them of this through a dream. It may also be understood in the manner of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, who would pray for the sick and then say, “This one will live and this one will die,” explaining, “If my prayer is fluent in my mouth,” etc., as stated in the chapter Ein Omdin.
text.7_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: “And I separated”—For they were now entering the wilderness route, Ezra entrusted the valuables to them because they were capable men who could guard them from enemies and ambushers along the way.
text.7_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: “And I weighed out to them; I weighed into their hands”—He first weighed the valuables, and afterward they weighed them a second time. The same procedure is found in Jeremiah [32:9–10]. “By talents”—each item was weighed according to the weight of a talent.
text.7_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: “Worth one thousand darics”—They were worth one thousand darics. “Golden-colored”—having a yellow appearance. The word occurs here in both masculine and feminine forms, because “vessel” is masculine, while “copper” is feminine.
text.7_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: “You are holy,” etc.—That is, you are responsible for safeguarding them, as it is written, “You shall keep the charge of the sacred things.”
text.7_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: “The chambers”—The preposition bet in “in Jerusalem” also applies to the following phrase: “in the chambers of the House of Hashem.”
text.7_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: “By number”—This refers both to their number and to their weight. They recorded the weight as well, and certainly the number of the items.
text.7_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: “All as a burnt offering”—We have already explained [on 6:17] that this was a temporary ruling.
text.7_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: “To the satraps”—We have already explained [on 7:11] that the letter was also addressed to the various peoples. Each people had satraps and a governor appointed by the king, as I explained in my commentary on the Book of Esther. They delivered to them the king’s decree, which was addressed to them as well.
text.8_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “And when these things were completed”—This did not occur until four months after his arrival, as will be seen below [10:9]. “They have not separated themselves”—That is, there was no distinction between them and the peoples of the lands: first, because they acted in accordance with their abominations.
text.8_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Second, “for they have taken some of their daughters for themselves.” Scripture uses the word “for” because marrying their daughters was what caused them to act according to their abominations. “And the hand of the officials”—they were the first to commit this trespass.
text.8_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: “Desolate and solitary”—as in, “And I sat there among them, stunned, for seven days” [Ezekiel 3].
text.8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: “Everyone who trembled”—The construction of the verse is: “Everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel concerning the transgression of the exiles,” for the verb “trembled” is not found joined with the preposition “concerning.”
text.8_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “I am ashamed and humiliated”—I have explained elsewhere that shame arises from oneself, whereas humiliation comes from others. Ezra explains “I am ashamed” by saying, “for our iniquities have multiplied above our head.” Iniquity is a distortion of the intellect, which resides in the head; their iniquities had risen above the head and spread outward. For this, one feels shame in oneself. Corresponding to “and humiliated,” he says, “and our guilt has grown up to the heavens.” Guilt entails liability to punishment, through which they suffered humiliation from others. [See what I have written on Isaiah, chapter 54.]
text.8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: “Since the days”—He added that their liability to punishment had not arisen only now. Rather, since the days of our fathers, the measure of sin had become full, and they had remained liable to punishment until this very day. Their being delivered into the hands of the kings of the lands had occurred because of their iniquities. Accordingly, given the extent of their sins and their liability to punishment, the appointed time of redemption had not yet arrived. The angel revealed this to Daniel, as stated [Daniel 9:24], “Seventy weeks have been decreed upon your people.” Israel’s return during the Second Temple period was only a temporary act of grace, while they still needed to purge their sins. This is the meaning of the following:
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “And now, for a brief moment, grace has been shown”—This was merely an act of grace, not something deserved by merit or strict justice, and it would last only for a brief moment. “To leave”—Ezra explains that this grace consisted of four things: first, “to leave us a remnant,” so that they would not be utterly destroyed in exile; second, “to give us a stake in His holy place,” enabling them to rebuild the Temple and establish their return to the Land of Israel; third, “that our God may enlighten our eyes,” for through this He could enlighten their eyes so that they would return to walking in His ways, thereby bringing the punishment decreed upon them to an end; and fourth, “to grant us a little sustenance,” enabling them to prosper to some extent while dwelling in their Land, although they remained “in our servitude,” for the time of the true redemption had not yet arrived, as the angel told Daniel.
text.8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “For”—He explains that we are still servants of the Persian kings, yet in our servitude He has not forsaken us, etc. This redemption was not complete, for it occurred only with the permission of the Persian kings and as an act of grace from Hashem: first, “to grant us sustenance”; second, “to raise up the House of our God”, by causing the decree authorizing the Temple’s construction to be issued; third, “to establish”—that is, to preserve the structure so that it would not be destroyed through the efforts of the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, who had written an accusation against its construction; and fourth, “to give us a wall”, enabling them to remain separate from the gentiles, like something enclosed within its own boundary. They had their own governor and leaders, as well as their own judges, so that they constituted a distinct people.
text.8_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “And now”—That is, since this was still not a complete redemption and their earlier sins had not yet been purged, the purpose of this redemption was that they should now improve their conduct and purge those sins. As the angel told Daniel, “Seventy weeks have been decreed upon your people, to terminate transgression and atone for iniquity.” They now had to atone for their earlier transgressions, as we explained there. If so, “what shall we say now?”—when we have done the opposite: not only have we failed to correct our earlier sins, but we have added new sins as well.
text.8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “An impure land”—For He told them that the land had been defiled by the abominations of the Canaanites, as it is written: “For through all these the nations that I am casting out before you became defiled. The land became defiled, and I visited its iniquity upon it, and the land vomited out its inhabitants” (Leviticus 18:24–25).
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: “And now, your daughters”—as it is written, “Lest you make a covenant with them and take from their daughters for your sons” (Exodus 34:16). Their inheritance of the Land and continued existence upon it depended upon observing this commandment, as stated in Joshua, chapter 23.
text.8_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: “And after all that has come upon us—for You, our God, have withheld”—That is, You restrained and held back the calamity coming upon us, so that it fell short of what our iniquities deserved. Because You restrained it, the calamity was less severe than was warranted by our sins, and by thus withholding it, You granted us such a remnant.
text.8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “Shall we again”—This refers back to what precedes: after all that has come upon us, how can we again violate Your commandments? Will You not be angry with us? Through this, will You not exhaust the full force of Your wrath against us—for the verb “to be angry” denotes the complete outpouring of wrath—until no remnant or survivor remains to us?
text.8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “O Hashem, God of Israel, You are righteous”—This applies both to the past, “for we have remained as a surviving remnant,” meaning that the punishment was less severe than our sins deserved, as stated, “You have withheld punishment beneath what our iniquities deserved”; this was because of Your righteousness. It also applies to the future, should You now become angry with us to the point of total destruction, “for behold, we are before You in our guilt.” Having become guilty once again, “for no one”—that is, because of this transgression of marrying foreign women, it is impossible “to stand before You” and offer any further claim in our defense.
text.9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: “Men, women, and children”—It may be that women whose husbands had taken foreign wives also assembled there, and they too wept, as Malachi—who is identified with Ezra—said concerning this: “And this second thing you do: you cover the altar of Hashem with tears.”
text.9_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: From that point onward, this transgression was attributed to everyone because they failed to protest it. Nevertheless, there was now hope of rectifying the matter, something they had previously lacked the power to do, because—
text.9_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: “And now, let us make a covenant with our God, according to the counsel of Hashem and of those who tremble at His commandments, to send away all the women and those born from them.” They knew that many would oppose them and refuse to send away their wives. Ezra possessed authority to punish only according to Torah law, whereas he now needed to frighten them with penalties more severe than those prescribed by law. The community has the power to impose such penalties if its members accept the matter by oath, for the community then possesses the authority of a king, who may impose punishments beyond the strict law, as seen in the incident of the concubine at Gibeah and elsewhere. Therefore, he proposed that they all enter into a covenant and unite with him in accepting the matter through an oath and imprecation. Then “let it be done according to the law”—they could punish anyone who violated it by virtue of the authority of the collective body of Israel, just as a severe punishment was imposed upon the people of Jabesh-gilead for violating the congregation’s oath.
text.9_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: “Then Ezra arose”—Ezra therefore administered the oath to the leaders of the priests and to the leaders of all Israel, so that the matter was enacted with the consent of the entire community.
text.9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: “And he went—and when he went there”—That is, even after he went there, he still ate no bread. Although the fast had ended, he was mourning over the exiles’ transgression and could not bring himself to eat.
text.9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “All his property shall be confiscated”—This penalty derived its authority from the collective enactment described above [verse 3]. Therefore, it was imposed “in accordance with the counsel of the officials and the elders,” for the community possesses the power to enact such a penalty.
text.9_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “Trembling”—both because of the matter—that is, the transgression—and because of the rains.
text.9_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “You have acted treacherously”—Since all Israel are responsible for one another, the guilt rested upon the entire community. Ezra wanted everyone to consent to the enactment, so that anyone who violated it would separate himself from the community. The community would then possess the authority of a king to punish him, whether by death or by eradication.
text.9_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “Let them remain”—That is, the leaders of the people should remain in Jerusalem on behalf of the entire congregation and in their place, so that whatever they did would be considered as having been done by the congregation as a whole. “Until this matter”—that is, until all the breaches of the generation were repaired, including this breach, so that no matter would remain for which Hashem’s anger might be kindled against them.
text.9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: “Only Jonathan”—Only these two opposed the matter contentiously, and two others supported them; the rest of the people, however, consented to it.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they separated themselves”—That is, Ezra and the heads of the ancestral houses remained in Jerusalem, separated from the people who had returned to their affairs, and they sat to investigate the matter.
text.9_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they finished with all”—[Scripture explains:] “with the men”—the preposition bet applies to both words, and therefore the word bakol is vocalized with a holam, as Ibn Ezra explains. “Who had married”—that is, who had caused foreign women to dwell with them. “And being guilty, they offered a ram from the flock”—Our Sages explained in Keritot 11a that they had relations with a designated maidservant and were therefore legally obligated to bring a ram as a guilt offering. This explains the words “and being guilty,” because one is liable for relations with a designated maidservant only if he had relations in the ordinary manner and completed the act. Therefore, if two witnesses said to him, “You had relations with a designated maidservant,” and he replied, “I did not,” he is not liable, since his response may mean, “I did not complete the act,” as explained in Keritot 12a. Consequently, witnesses alone could not obligate him to bring a ram as a guilt offering; rather, the men themselves admitted that they were guilty and thus obligated to bring a ram from the flock. Although they could have freed these women, the men were priests, and the women would have remained forbidden to them as women who had engaged in prohibited relations. They therefore pledged, under a conditional vow, to send them away, following the law governing a priest who married a woman forbidden to him: he makes a vow to divorce her and may then perform the Temple service. Rashi writes that this was a temporary ruling, but this is difficult, because it contradicts the Gemara cited above. It appears that Rashi follows his own position in Gittin 36a that the Jubilee was not observed during the Second Temple period. Since the accepted law identifies the designated maidservant as one betrothed to a Hebrew slave, such a case could not have occurred during the Second Temple period, because Hebrew slavery applies only when the Jubilee is observed. Rav Hisda’s statement that they had relations with designated maidservants must therefore follow the opinion of Aherim in Keritot 11a, which identifies her as a maidservant betrothed to a Canaanite slave, an opinion that does not accord with the law according to Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ishmael, who maintain that she is betrothed to a Hebrew slave. Tosafot in Gittin and Arakhin [31b], however, write that the Jubilee was observed during the Second Temple period and that Hebrew slavery therefore applied. According to their view, Rav Hisda’s explanation accords with the accepted law.
text.9_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: “Of the descendants of Bani”—They were already enumerated [in verse 29], unless these were the grandchildren of Bani.
text.9_Chapter, 43_Verse, 0_Comment: “And some of them had wives”—The word “had married” applies to both parts of the statement: some had married foreign wives, and they had produced children. Scripture does not say “and they had begotten children,” because the child of a non-Jewish woman has her status.
